claims.text: The investigated particles are sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The initial nanoparticles have elliptical or icosahedral morphology.
The PLD-grown AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles possess a metastable FCC structure governed by kinetic effects.
Surface energy anisotropy and curvature generate chemical-potential gradients in sub-5 nm nanoparticles.
These gradients lower the activation barrier for Au and Cu surface diffusion relative to bulk diffusion.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of sub-5 nm particles makes the surface-energy term dominate their behavior.
Au and Cu have sufficiently low surface energies to segregate to the nanoparticle surface and reduce total free energy.
Element-dependent atomic mobility can remain substantial in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Surface diffusion is less hindered by sluggish lattice diffusion than bulk diffusion is.
Surface accumulation of Au and Cu causes their evaporation.
Au and Cu evaporation causes particle shrinkage, preferential loss of sub-5 nm particles, and widening of the size distribution.
The transition from elliptical to spherical particles is driven by surface-area minimization under surface-energy gradients.
A critical temperature exists above which Au/Cu surface segregation and evaporation outpace bulk diffusion.
Icosahedral particles will reshape and lose mass faster than truncated-octahedral particles because they have higher surface energy.
Surface-energy gradients alone can reproduce the observed phase separation without invoking sluggish bulk diffusion.
The proposed mechanism applies only below a nanoparticle diameter of 10 nm, where surface terms dominate bulk thermodynamic terms.
In bulk alloys and nanoparticles larger than 10 nm, bulk diffusion and entropy stabilization are the primary drivers.
Sluggish diffusion can suppress microstructural growth in refractory multicomponent alloy films.
The exact critical temperature is unknown because direct surface-diffusion coefficients are unavailable for this quinary nanoparticle system.

Failure of surface-energy-only simulations to reproduce Au/Cu segregation and evaporation, or absence of a relationship between initial shape and degradation rate, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
